title: The Conjurer after Bosch: the trick, the thief and the frog nobody notices
question: A trick, a crowd, a man leaning in too far. Who in this picture is really being played?

seo.meta_title: The Conjurer (after Bosch): the Trick, the Thief, the Frog
seo.meta_description: A guided zoom through The Conjurer, after Hieronymus Bosch (c. 1502): the cups-and-balls trick, the pickpocket, the frog, the owl and the dog in a hood.

intro: The Conjurer is a painting from around 1502, attributed to Hieronymus Bosch or his workshop, in the municipal museum of Saint-Germain-en-Laye near Paris. Bosch's original is lost; this is considered a very good copy. A street magician performs the cups-and-balls trick for a crowd. While one well-dressed man leans in, spellbound, a man behind him quietly steals his purse. Everyone is watching the wrong thing.

sections.heading: The oldest trick
paragraphs: On the right, the conjurer in red stands at his table with cups, little balls and a wand: the cups-and-balls trick, still performed by street magicians today. He holds up a small ball, a pearl, between his fingers, and every eye follows it.
That is exactly what he wants. The painting is not about the trick but about attention: about how easily people are fooled when they stop paying attention to what matters.

sections.heading: Look behind the leaning man
paragraphs: The central figure is a man of rank, leaning so far over the table that he is almost falling. He is fixed on the pearl. Behind him, a man in spectacles looks innocently up at the sky, while his hand removes the purse hanging from the leaning man's belt.

A small boy has noticed. He grins at the victim, not at the trick. A Flemish proverb said it plainly: whoever lets himself be fooled by conjuring tricks loses his money and becomes the laughing stock of children.

sections.heading: A frog in his mouth
paragraphs: Bosch adds his own strangeness. A frog jumps out of the leaning man's open mouth, and another sits on the table: a sign of how completely he has let go of reason. In the conjurer's basket, a little owl peeks out, a symbol of the trickster's cunning. At his feet sits a small dog dressed in a hood with ears, like a performer's animal.
Animals in the painting stand for the human failings that make the trick work: foolishness on one side, cleverness on the other.

sections.heading: Lost, copied and stolen
paragraphs: Bosch's own painting is lost. Tree-ring analysis of the panel in Saint-Germain-en-Laye dates it to around 1502, and it is regarded as a faithful version from Bosch's workshop or circle. The museum keeps it locked in a safe and lends it only for special exhibitions.
It has been the victim of a trick itself: it was stolen from the museum on 1 December 1978 and recovered on 2 February 1979.

meaning: The message is a warning: the conjurer is a common criminal, and the crowd are his prey.
But Bosch spreads the blame. The thief steals, the conjurer distracts, and the victim makes it easy by giving his full attention to a pearl. The only one who sees the whole picture is a child.
whereToSee: Musée municipal, Saint-Germain-en-Laye, France. The painting is kept in a safe and shown mainly in special exhibitions; check with the museum before you visit.

details.headline: A street show, around 1502
details.text: A magician, a table, a crowd. Everyone is watching the trick. Let's watch everything else.

details.headline: The conjurer
details.text: On the right, a man in red with a tall black hat holds up a tiny ball between his fingers. Every eye in the crowd follows it.

details.headline: The pearl
details.text: Look at his hand: a small pearl, raised just high enough to be seen. That is the whole trick.

details.headline: Cups and balls
details.text: On the table: cups, little balls and a wand. The cups-and-balls trick, still performed in streets today.

details.headline: The man leaning in
details.text: A well-dressed man leans so far over the table that he is about to fall into it. Completely spellbound.

details.headline: A frog in his mouth
details.text: Look at his face: a frog is jumping out of his open mouth. Bosch's way of saying he has lost his mind.

details.headline: Another frog
details.text: And there is a second frog, sitting on the table among the conjurer's things.

details.headline: The innocent look
details.text: Behind the victim, a man in spectacles gazes up at the sky, as if thinking about something else entirely.

details.headline: The hand
details.text: But follow his arm down: his hand is lifting the purse from the leaning man's belt. Everyone is watching the wrong thing.

details.headline: The child sees
details.text: Under the table's edge, a little boy with a toy windmill grins at the victim. He is the only one who has noticed.

details.headline: An owl in the basket
details.text: Hanging from the conjurer's belt, a wicker basket. Inside, a little owl peeks out: the symbol of his cunning.

details.headline: A dog in costume
details.text: At his feet, a small dog sits in a hood with pointed ears, like a performer's animal waiting for its cue.

details.headline: The audience
details.text: Behind them, a whole row of faces: a nun, young men, a woman in red, a man in green. All looking at the trick.

details.headline: Who are you watching?
details.text: The trick, the thief or the child? A proverb of the time said that whoever falls for conjuring tricks loses his money and becomes the laughing stock of children.

The thief in spectacles: Wikipedia says 'a man is stealing the purse'; the spectacles and upward gaze are what the image shows.
The dog in a hood, the nun, the toy windmill: described visually, not in the source.
